passages.t: One in love: look to the interests of others
passages.happening:
Paul makes an appeal. “Therefore if you have any encouragement in Christ, if any comfort from His love, if any fellowship with the Spirit, if any affection and compassion, then make my joy complete by being like-minded, having the same love, being united in spirit and purpose” (verses 1-2).

He says how: “Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride, but in humility consider others more important than yourselves” (verse 3). “Each of you should look not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The four ‘if’ clauses are not doubts. They mean ‘since’. Since you have known Christ's encouragement, his love, the Spirit's fellowship, then live like it with one another.

The church in Philippi had a problem with unity. Later Paul names two women leaders who were at odds (4:2). Here he speaks to everyone, before he names anyone.

In the Greek and Roman world humility was not usually admired. The word often described the mean attitude of the lowly, people who did not matter. Honour and status were things to be chased openly. Paul makes humility a virtue, and he will show in the next verses where it comes from: from Christ himself.

Notice what humility is, and is not. It is not thinking you are worthless. Paul says ‘consider others more important’, not ‘consider yourself nothing’. And notice verse 4: ‘not only to your own interests, but also’. Paul does not tell anyone to have no interests at all. He tells them to make room for the interests of others. A church where everyone does that is a church at peace.
passages.ot:
Proverbs says God is on the side of the humble: “He mocks the mockers, but gives grace to the humble” (Proverbs 3:34).

The law already asked God's people to look to the good of others: “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). And Micah gave the shape of a life that pleases God: “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” (Micah 6:8).
passages.asks: Paul asks you to look to the interests of others. Think of one person close to you. Ask what their interests are this week, and whether you know. Ask where selfish ambition or empty pride is at work in you. And ask whether your humility is real, or only a low opinion of yourself that still keeps you at the centre.

passages.t: The mind of Christ: he emptied himself, and God exalted him
passages.happening:
“Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” (verse 5). Then Paul tells the story of Christ in a song that goes down, then up.

Down: “Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness. And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death— even death on a cross” (verses 6-8).

Up: “Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
These verses are written in a rhythm that sets them apart from the rest of the letter. Many scholars think they are an early Christian hymn that Paul quotes, perhaps one the Philippians already sang. Others think Paul wrote them himself. Either way, Paul uses them for a practical reason: to show the church how to treat one another.

In the first half Christ is the one acting. He did not grasp. He emptied himself. He humbled himself. Step by step he goes down: from the form of God to the form of a servant, the Greek word for a slave; from servant to death; from death to the worst death of all.

That last step would hit the Philippians hard. Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, made to shame as much as to kill. Roman citizens, like many in Philippi, were normally spared it. ‘Even death on a cross’ is the bottom of the song.

In the second half God is the one acting. He exalted Jesus and gave him ‘the name above all names’. That name is ‘Lord’. In a city that honoured the emperor with the titles of a god and hailed him as saviour, this was a bold thing to sing. The one who went lowest is the one God raised highest.
passages.ot:
The end of the song takes up words from Isaiah, where the LORD, the God of Israel, says, “By Myself I have sworn; truth has gone out from My mouth, a word that will not be revoked: Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance” (Isaiah 45:23). In Isaiah the knees bow to the LORD, who says “I am God, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:22). In Philippians they bow at the name of Jesus. The song gives to Jesus the honour that belongs to Israel's one God.

The song also sounds like Isaiah's servant. “Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted” (Isaiah 52:13). He is exalted “because He has poured out His life unto death” (Isaiah 53:12).

And some readers hear Adam behind the song. Adam and Eve were tempted to grasp at being “like God” (Genesis 3:5). Christ, who truly was equal with God, did not grasp.
passages.hard:
When Christ ‘emptied Himself’, did he stop being God?

No. Here these notes do not set out one view among several. They state what the church confesses. The Nicene Creed confesses the Son as ‘very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father’, who ‘came down from heaven’ and ‘was made man’. The Council of Chalcedon in AD 451 confessed him as ‘truly God and truly man’, one person in two natures, ‘without confusion, without change, without division, without separation’. This song is one of the places that confession comes from.

The song itself shows what the emptying means. It explains ‘emptied Himself’ by what he took: ‘taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness’. He did not lay down being God. He took up being man. What he set aside was clinging to the honour and rights that were his. And at the end he receives the worship Isaiah gives to the LORD alone, which would make no sense if he had stopped being God.

Christians still think hard about how the Son's divine and human life fit together: how he could grow in wisdom (Luke 2:52), or say that he did not know the day of his return (Mark 13:32). Some theologians in the 1800s proposed that the Son laid aside certain powers of God, such as knowing all things, in order to live a truly human life. Many who hold such ideas mean to keep the creeds. Others answer that he kept every power of God but chose not to use them for himself. These are questions asked within the faith. But any teaching that Christ ceased to be God, or was only partly God while he lived on earth, steps outside what the church has always confessed. The site's chapter note on Philippians 2 says more.
passages.asks: Paul tells this story so that the church will treat one another the way Christ treated us. Ask what rights or honours you hold on to tightly. Ask where you could take the lower place for someone else's good. And ask whether you have bowed the knee to Jesus as Lord, not someday, but now.

passages.t: Work out your salvation; shine like stars
passages.happening:
“Therefore, my beloved, just as you have always obeyed, not only in my presence, but now even more in my absence, continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose” (verses 12-13).

“Do everything without complaining or arguing” (verse 14), so that they may be “children of God without fault in a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine as lights in the world as you hold forth the word of life” (verses 15-16).

Paul adds, “But even if I am being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with all of you” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
‘Therefore’ ties this to the song. Because Christ went down and was raised, live out the life he has given you.

‘Work out’ does not mean ‘work for’. It means to bring something to its full result, the way a farmer works a field until it gives its harvest. The Philippians already have salvation; it is ‘your salvation’. Paul tells them to live it out fully, in every part of life.

And the reason they can is verse 13. God is already at work in them, even in what they want (‘to will’) and in what they do (‘to act’). Their work does not compete with God's work. It is the result of it.

‘Fear and trembling’ is not terror that God will reject them. It is the awe of people who know that the living God is at work inside them.

‘Lights in the world’ may also be translated ‘stars’. In a dark and twisted world, the church shines simply by being different: not grumbling, not arguing, holding out the word of life.

The ‘drink offering’ was wine poured out beside a sacrifice, in Israel's worship and in the worship of the Greeks and Romans too. Paul pictures his possible death as that kind of offering, poured out on top of the Philippians' own faithful service. He is glad to be spent for them.
passages.ot:
Paul's words about grumbling and a ‘crooked and perverse generation’ echo Israel in the wilderness. Moses told the people, “Your grumblings are not against us but against the LORD” (Exodus 16:8). And the song of Moses mourned that Israel had become “a perverse and crooked generation” (Deuteronomy 32:5). Paul hopes the church will be what Israel in the desert was not.

‘Fear and trembling’ joined to joy is in the Psalms: “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11).

The stars recall Daniel: “those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12:3). And the drink offering is from Israel's worship: “Pour out the offering of fermented drink to the LORD in the sanctuary area” (Numbers 28:7).

Isaiah had said what Paul says in verse 13: “For all that we have accomplished, You have done for us” (Isaiah 26:12).
passages.hard:
Does ‘work out your salvation with fear and trembling’ mean we have to earn it, or keep it by our own effort?

No. Paul is writing to people who are already saved, and he calls it ‘your salvation’. Salvation is God's gift, by grace, through faith, as Ephesians 2:8-9 says and as the church confesses. ‘Work out’ means to live it out, not to win it.

Verse 13 holds the two sides together. We work, really and with effort, because God is at work in us. God's work does not make ours pointless, and ours does not add to his. Christians have described this in different words. Protestant churches stress that good works are the fruit of salvation and never its ground. Catholic and Orthodox churches stress that grace truly changes a person, so that works done in grace belong to the life God rewards. All agree that grace comes first and that no one can boast. The note on Ephesians 2:1-10 and the Romans book page set out the views; these notes do not choose.

If ‘fear and trembling’ has left you afraid that God is waiting for you to fail, hear the next verse. It is God who works in you. He began the good work, and he will finish it (1:6).
passages.asks: Paul says God is at work in you, in what you want and in what you do. Ask what part of your life you have not yet let your salvation reach. Ask whether you complain more than you give thanks. And ask what it would mean, where you live and work, to shine like a star in the dark.

passages.t: Timothy and Epaphroditus: two lives like Christ's
passages.happening:
Paul hopes to send Timothy soon (verse 19). “I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs. For all the others look after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (verses 20-21). “But you know Timothy’s proven worth, that as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel” (verse 22). Paul hopes to come himself soon too (verse 24).

Meanwhile he is sending back Epaphroditus, “my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my needs” (verse 25). Epaphroditus had been ill, “nearly unto death. But God had mercy on him, and not only on him but also on me, to spare me sorrow upon sorrow” (verse 27). “Welcome him in the Lord with great joy, and honor men like him, because he nearly died for the work of Christ, risking his life” (verses 29-30).
passages.hearers:
These are not just travel plans. They are two living pictures of the song in verses 5 to 11. Timothy looks to the interests of others (compare verse 4). Epaphroditus went near to death in service, as Christ ‘became obedient to death’.

Timothy had joined Paul shortly before the church in Philippi began (Acts 16:1-3), so they knew him well. Paul calls him a son. In that world a son learned his father's trade by working beside him, and that is what Timothy had done with Paul.

Epaphroditus was one of their own. The church had sent him with a gift for Paul and to stay and help him. Then he fell gravely ill. And notice what distressed him: not his own sickness, but that his church had heard about it and would be worried (verse 26).

The word Paul uses for ‘risking’ his life comes from gambling: staking everything on one throw. Epaphroditus staked his life on serving Christ.

And notice how honest Paul is. Epaphroditus was not healed at once; he nearly died. When he recovered, Paul called it mercy, not something owed. And Paul admits his own fear of ‘sorrow upon sorrow’ and says he will be ‘less anxious’ (verse 28) once Epaphroditus is home. Even an apostle worried, and said so.
passages.ot:
Friendship that stays through hard times is praised in Proverbs: “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Proverbs 17:17).

God's mercy to the sick has a long history in Scripture. When King Hezekiah was dying, God said through Isaiah, “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life” (Isaiah 38:5). Like Paul, the Old Testament calls recovery a mercy from God, not a right.

And the servant who gives himself for others is Isaiah's servant again, who says, “I offered My back to those who struck Me” (Isaiah 50:6).
passages.asks: Paul says he has no one else like Timothy, who genuinely cares. Ask whether anyone could say that of you. Ask who has risked something to serve you, and whether you have honoured them. And if you are worried about someone you love, notice that Paul did not hide his worry. Bring yours to God, and to people who care.
